analysis.title: A brake on the highway: Asia's AI suppliers face rising US midterm election policy risk
key_insights: The recent market rout is testing faith in Asia's AI growth in equities and exports. The main concern has shifted from securing chips to who can fund the expansion and overcome energy bottlenecks.
Democratic gains in the US midterm election could add another brake if they strengthen support for tighter data-center permitting and electricity rules in 2027.
For cloud service providers, slower construction and grid approvals could leave already-purchased semiconductors idle, and any double booking would amplify the adjustment.
Persistent delays could lead providers to use accumulated stocks first and defer new purchases. That would ease cash outflows but postpone revenue growth.
Strong AI adoption offers support, but the 2018 crypto-GPU glut and the 2022-23 memory slump caution against assuming 'this time is different'.
Asian server assemblers and networking suppliers appear most exposed to near-term order cuts.
Korean memory producers could face weaker HBM demand, plus separate Chinese competition in conventional memory.
Taiwan's mature-node suppliers serving data centers could face pressure on volumes and prices.
Leading-edge foundries and advanced packaging suppliers have stronger pricing power because customers have fewer alternatives.

Regulatory divergence is a partial offset. If tighter US rules make data centers slower or costlier to build, some new investment could move to Asian markets with faster approvals and competitive infrastructure costs. Energy bottlenecks, construction lead times and the smaller market size relative to the US mean this cannot fully offset the hit.

tension_points.bear_case: Tighter US data-center permitting and electricity rules in 2027 could slow construction, leave purchased chips idle and cut near-term orders. The 2018 crypto-GPU glut and 2022-23 memory slump show demand can reverse.
